# Social insurance and poor relief (`social_insurance`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by insurance, life_tables_annuities, census_vital_registration, progressive_income_tax
- Core idea: Workers and employers pay small regular contributions into a common fund, by legal obligation; the fund pays a fixed benefit in sickness, after accidents, in old age and to widows and orphans. Compulsion is the key: a voluntary scheme attracts mainly those who expect to claim and fails, while a fund covering everyone spreads the risk and is cheap per head. It needs registers of members and their ages, mortality and sickness tables to set contributions, and funds kept apart from the treasury. Where wage records do not exist, begin with guild, parish or miners' mutual funds and public granaries.
- Pitfalls:
  - Promising benefits without tables of how many will claim: early schemes went bankrupt or set the pension age beyond most lifetimes
  - Saying Bismarck set retirement at 65: the 1889 law paid from age 70; 65 came in 1916
  - A fund the ruler can borrow from is spent on war
  - Relief that is paid only to the destitute and withdrawn on any earnings discourages work; relief tied to the home parish stops people moving to where work is
  - Thinking welfare is a modern invention: Roman grain doles, Islamic zakat, Chinese granaries and Inca storehouses all fed people on a large scale
- History: rome: 123 BC – Gaius Gracchus' subsidised grain for citizens, free from 58 BC; c. AD 100 Trajan's alimenta, loan interest paying for poor children in Italian towns; burial clubs (collegia); china: 54 BC – ever-normal granaries proposed by Geng Shouchang; Song (11th–12th c.) state poorhouses, charity clinics and paupers' cemeteries; 1168 Zhu Xi's community granary; india: c. 250 BC – Ashoka's edicts record medical care, wells and shade trees for people and animals; temple and guild charity; islamic: 7th c. – zakat, an obligatory levy on wealth for the poor, debtors and travellers; treasury stipends under Umar; later waqf-funded hospitals and soup kitchens; americas: 15th c. – Inca state storehouses (qollqa) feed labourers, the old and the widowed and cover bad harvests; europe: c. 1260 – miners' mutual funds (Knappschaften) in the Harz; 1601 English Poor Law, parish rates for the poor; 18th c. friendly societies; 1883–1889 Bismarck's sickness, accident and old-age insurance; 1911 British National Insurance; 1942 Beveridge Report
- Read:
  - E. P. Hennock, The Origin of the Welfare State in England and Germany, 1850–1914 (2007)
  - William Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services (1942)
